facts.quote: type_species_authority: (Lü et al., 2004)

facts.statement: Nemegtomaia lived in what is now Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous Period, approximately 72 to 70 million years ago.
facts.quote: Nemegtomaia is a genus of oviraptorid dinosaur from what is now Mongolia that lived in the Late Cretaceous Period, about 72 to 70 million years ago.

facts.statement: The first specimen of Nemegtomaia was discovered in 1996.
facts.quote: The first specimen was found in 1996

facts.statement: Two additional specimens of Nemegtomaia were discovered in 2007.
facts.quote: Two more specimens were found in 2007

facts.statement: Nemegtomaia is estimated to have been about 2 meters (7 feet) long and weighed 40 kilograms (85 pounds).
facts.quote: Nemegtomaia is estimated to have been around 2 m (7 ft) in length, and to have weighed 40 kg (85 lb).

facts.statement: As an oviraptorosaur, Nemegtomaia would have been covered in feathers.
facts.quote: As an oviraptorosaur, it would have been feathered.

facts.statement: Nemegtomaia had a deep, narrow, and short skull featuring an arched crest.
facts.quote: It had a deep, narrow, and short skull, with an arched crest.

facts.statement: Nemegtomaia had three fingers, with the first being the largest and bearing a strong claw.
facts.quote: It had three fingers; the first was largest and bore a strong claw.

facts.statement: The eggs associated with the nesting specimen were estimated to be 5 to 6 cm wide and 14 to 16 cm long when intact.
facts.quote: None of the eggs are complete, but they are estimated to have been 5 to 6 cm (2 to 2.3 in) wide and 14 to 16 cm (5 to 6 in) long when intact.

facts.statement: Damage on the nesting specimen's skeleton indicates it was scavenged by skin beetles.
facts.quote: The skeleton of the nesting specimen has damage that indicates it was scavenged by skin beetles.

facts.statement: The diet of oviraptorids is uncertain, though their skulls resemble those of known or suspected herbivores.
facts.quote: The diet of oviraptorids is uncertain, but their skulls are most similar to other animals that are known or thought to have been herbivorous.

facts.statement: Nemegtomaia fossils are found in the Nemegt and Baruungoyot formations, which represent both humid and arid environments that coexisted.
facts.quote: Nemegtomaia is known from the Nemegt and Baruungoyot formations, which are thought to represent humid and arid environments that coexisted in the same area.

facts.statement: In 1996, Yoshitsugu Kobayashi found an incomplete oviraptorid skeleton in the Nemegt Formation of the Gobi Desert in southwestern Mongolia.
facts.quote: In 1996 the palaeontologist Yoshitsugu Kobayashi (as part of the "Mongolian Highland International Dinosaur Project" team) found an incomplete skeleton of an oviraptorid dinosaur in the Nemegt Formation of the Gobi Desert in southwestern Mongolia.

facts.statement: In 2002, Lü Junchang and colleagues described the first specimen as an uncertain species of the genus Ingenia.
facts.quote: The specimen was described as a new specimen of the genus Ingenia (referred to as Ingenia sp.; of uncertain species) by the palaeontologist Lü Junchang and colleagues in 2002

facts.statement: In 2004, Lü and colleagues designated the skeleton as the holotype for the new species Nemegtia barsboldi.
facts.quote: In 2004 Lü and colleagues determined that the skeleton belonged to a new, distinct taxon, and made it the holotype specimen of Nemegtia barsboldi.

facts.statement: In 2005, researchers discovered that the name Nemegtia was preoccupied by a genus of freshwater seed shrimp described in 1978.
facts.quote: In 2005 the describers discovered (after being notified by a biologist) that the name Nemegtia had already been used for a genus of freshwater seed shrimp (Ostracoda) from the same formation in 1978, and was therefore preoccupied.

facts.statement: Two new specimens were found in 2007 and formally described by Federico Fanti and colleagues in 2013.
facts.quote: In 2007 two new specimens of Nemegtomaia were found by the "Dinosaurs of the Gobi" expedition, and were described by the palaeontologist Federico Fanti and colleagues in 2013.

facts.statement: The first of the new specimens, nicknamed "Mary", was found by Federico Fanti in the Baruungoyot Formation.
facts.quote: The first specimen, MPC-D 107/15, was found by Fanti (who nicknamed it "Mary") in the Baruungoyot Formation

facts.statement: The second new specimen was discovered by Nicholas R. Longrich in the Nemegt Formation.
facts.quote: The second specimen, MPC-D 107/16, was found by the palaeontologist Nicholas R. Longrich in the Nemegt Formation

facts.statement: Nemegtomaia had a well-developed crest formed mainly by the premaxilla bones of the snout.
facts.quote: It had a well-developed crest, formed by the nasal and premaxilla bones (mainly the latter) of the snout.

facts.statement: The diameter of the eye opening was 52 mm (2 in), making the eyes appear large due to the short skull.
facts.quote: The diameter of the orbit (eye opening) was 52 mm (2 in); the eyes looked large due to the shortness of the skull.

facts.statement: Nemegtomaia had toothless jaws with a short snout featuring a deep, robust, parrot-like beak.
facts.quote: The jaws of Nemegtomaia were toothless, and like other oviraptorid dinosaurs, it had a short snout with a deep, robust, and somewhat parrot-like beak.

facts.statement: Small openings on the snout suggest the presence of a keratinous bill.
facts.quote: Nemegtomaia had small foramina (openings) on the sides of the suture (joint) between the premaxillae at the front of the snout, which may have been nutrient openings (and which indicate the presence of a keratinous bill).

facts.statement: The lower jaw was short, deep, and convex, reaching 153 mm (6 in) in length.
facts.quote: The lower jaw was short and deep, with a convex lower surface, and reached 153 mm (6 in) in length.

facts.statement: The shoulder blade of Nemegtomaia was approximately 185 mm (7 in) long.
facts.quote: The scapula (shoulder blade) appears to have been 185 mm (7 in) in total length.

facts.statement: The upper arm bone had a bird-like depression and measured 152 mm (6 in) in length.
facts.quote: The humerus (upper arm bone) had a fossa (depression) in a position similar to modern birds, but atypical among oviraptorosaurs, and appears to have been 152 mm (6 in) long.

facts.statement: The first finger was large, had a strong claw, and was more massive than the other two fingers.
facts.quote: The first finger was relatively large and had a strong ungual (claw bone), and was more massive than the two other fingers.

facts.statement: The thigh bone was estimated to be 286 mm (11 in) long, while the lower leg bone was 317 mm (12 in) long.
facts.quote: The femur (thigh bone) is estimated to have been 286 mm (11 in) long, and the tibia of the lower leg 317 mm long (12 in).

facts.statement: In 2004, Lü and colleagues classified Nemegtomaia as an advanced oviraptorosaur most closely related to Citipati.
facts.quote: In their 2004 phylogenetic analysis, Lü and colleagues classified Nemegtomaia as a derived (or "advanced") oviraptorosaur, and found it to be most closely related to the genus Citipati.

facts.statement: In 2010, Longrich and colleagues placed Nemegtomaia in the family Oviraptoridae and subfamily Ingeniinae, noting it was the only member of that subfamily with a prominent crest.
facts.quote: In 2010 Longrich and colleagues determined that Nemegtomaia belonged in the family Oviraptoridae, as part of the subfamily Ingeniinae, making it the only member of the latter group with a prominent crest.

facts.statement: Longrich and colleagues suggested that the crest might have evolved or disappeared multiple times among oviraptorids, or that Nemegtomaia may not belong to the subfamily Ingeniinae.
facts.quote: Longrich and colleagues suggested that the presence of a crest on Nemegtomaia makes it possible that this feature evolved or disappeared several times among oviraptorids, or that the animal may not have been an ingeniine.

facts.statement: In 2012, Fanti and colleagues classified Nemegtomaia as a derived member of Ingeniinae closest to Heyuannia based on hand proportions.
facts.quote: In 2012 Fanti and colleagues also found Nemegtomaia to be part of Ingeniinae as a derived member, closest to Heyuannia, due to the proportions of the hands of the two new specimens (relatively short with a robust first finger).

facts.statement: The subfamily name Ingeniinae has been replaced by Heyuanninae due to nomenclatural preoccupation.
facts.quote: The subfamily name Ingeniinae has since been replaced by the name Heyuanninae (since Ingenia was preoccupied).

facts.statement: Oviraptorosaurs, including Nemegtomaia, are known from Asia and North America and date to the Campanian-Maastrichtian ages of the Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Oviraptorosaurs are known from Asia (where they may have originated) and North America, and are mainly known from deposits that date from the Campanian-Maastrichtian ages of the Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: The family Oviraptoridae, to which Nemegtomaia belongs, consists of small members known exclusively from the Upper Cretaceous of Asia, particularly the Gobi Desert.
facts.quote: The family Oviraptoridae (to which Nemegtomaia belongs) consisted of generally small members, and is exclusively known from the Upper Cretaceous of Asia, with most genera having been discovered in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia and China.

facts.statement: Oviraptorosaurs are thought to have been feathered but flightless.
facts.quote: Though they are all thought to have been feathered, they appear to have been flightless.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul suggested that crestless oviraptorids were juveniles or females of crested species, implying the number of genera in the group was exaggerated.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul suggested that crestless oviraptorids were either the juveniles or females of otherwise crested species, and that the number of genera in the group was therefore exaggerated.

facts.statement: The Nemegtomaia specimen MPC-D 107/15 was discovered in a brooding posture with its feet in the center of a ring of eggs and arms folded over them.
facts.quote: The Nemegtomaia specimen MPC-D 107/15 was found associated with a nest with eggs; its feet were placed in the centre of what was probably a ring of eggs, with the arms folded across the tops of the eggs on each side of the body

facts.statement: The preserved portion of the Nemegtomaia nest measured approximately 90 cm wide and 100 cm long.
facts.quote: The collected part of the nest is about 90 cm (35 in) wide and 100 cm (30 in) long

facts.statement: Seven distinct eggs and fragments were found in the Nemegtomaia nest, located under the skeleton or in the lower layer.
facts.quote: Most eggs (seven distinct eggs have been identified) and egg fragments were recovered either in the lower layer of the nest or under the skull, neck, and limbs of the specimen

facts.statement: Oviraptorid eggs, including those associated with Nemegtomaia, average about 17 cm in length.
facts.quote: Oviraptorid eggs appear to have been 17 cm (6 in) long on average

facts.statement: Eggs found with Nemegtomaia are similar to those from Mongolia and are classified in the egg family Elongatoolithidae.
facts.quote: The eggs are nearly identical to some that have previously been found in Mongolia, and have therefore been assigned to the oofamily (egg-taxon family) Elongatoolithidae

facts.statement: No complete eggs or embryos were preserved in the Nemegtomaia nest, preventing full analysis of egg size, shape, number, or arrangement.
facts.quote: The nest does not preserve any complete eggs or embryos, which prevents determination of the size, shape, number, and arrangement of the eggs in the nest

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the original nest likely had two layers of eggs beneath the body with no eggs in the center.
facts.quote: It is probable that there were originally two layers of eggs below the body, and there do not appear to have been eggs in the centre of the nest

facts.statement: Nemegtomaia likely nested near streams in otherwise dry environments to access soft sand and food.
facts.quote: The nesting specimen was found in a stratigraphic area indicating that oviraptorids preferred nesting near streams that provided soft, sandy substrate and food in environments that were otherwise xeric (receiving a small amount of moisture)

facts.statement: Some researchers propose that tail feathers in oviraptorosaurs evolved to shade and protect eggs in the nest.
facts.quote: It has also been suggested that the evolution of tail-feathers in oviraptorosaurs was an adaptation for shading and protecting eggs in their nests

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the cuticle coating on oviraptorid eggs helped enhance reproductive success in variable nesting environments.
facts.quote: The researchers suggested that the cuticle-coated eggs would have been a trait adapted for enhancing their reproductive success in the variable environments where Nemegtomaia and other oviraptorids nested

facts.statement: Studies suggest multiple individuals may have gathered eggs in a single nest to be guarded by one individual, possibly a male.
facts.quote: Various studies have suggested that several individuals would gather eggs in a single nest, and arrange them so they could be protected by one individual, possibly a male

facts.statement: David J. Varricchio and colleagues found in 2010 that oviraptorid clutch sizes resemble those of modern archosaurs with polygamous mating and extensive male parental care.
facts.quote: In 2010 the palaeontologist David J. Varricchio and colleagues found that the relatively large clutch-size of oviraptorids and troodontids is most similar to those of modern archosaurs (birds and crocodilians, the closest living relatives of dinosaurs) that practice polygamous mating and extensive male parental care

facts.statement: W. Scott Persons and colleagues suggested in 2013 that feather-fans on oviraptorosaur tails were used for intraspecific communication like courtship rituals.
facts.quote: Many oviraptorosaurs are known to have had pygostyles on the end of their tails, which suggests the presence of feather-fans; the palaeontologist W. Scott Persons and colleagues suggested in 2013 that these could have been used for intraspecific communication such as courtship rituals

facts.statement: In 2026, Chun-Yu Su and colleagues conducted an experiment to test if oviraptorids used thermoregulatory contact incubation.
facts.quote: The palaeontologist Chun-Yu Su and colleagues devised an experiment to evaluate whether oviraptorids employed thermoregulatory contact incubation to provide heat for embryonic development in 2026

facts.statement: Experiments showed that partial egg coverage in oviraptorid nests led to temperature differences and lower incubation efficiency compared to modern birds.
facts.quote: The results showed that the incubator only partially covered the eggs in the outer ring of the clutch, which led to a difference in temperature between the inner and outer eggs, and therefore lower incubation efficiency than in modern birds

facts.statement: Researchers concluded that oviraptorids likely co-regulated incubation using environmental and solar heat rather than body contact.
facts.quote: These researchers concluded that their experiment did not support thermoregulatory contact incubation in oviraptorids, instead suggesting they co-regulated their incubation with environmental heat (in conjunction with solar input)

facts.statement: It is debated whether oviraptorids had temperature-dependent sex determination, as temperature differences in nests might have skewed sex ratios.
facts.quote: The large difference between incubation temperatures in the two oviraptorids suggests they did not have temperature-dependent sex determination (which is used by for example crocodiles), as the sex-ratios would be skewed

facts.statement: Research published in 2010 suggested that the jaws of oviraptorids, including Nemegtomaia, shared features with herbivorous animals.
facts.quote: In 2010 Longrich and colleagues found that oviraptorid jaws had features similar to those seen in herbivorous tetrapods

facts.statement: A 2017 study proposed that the parrot-like jaws of oviraptorids might indicate a diet consisting of fruits, nuts, and seeds.

facts.statement: While R. Barsbold suggested in 1977 that oviraptorids ate molluscs, later research rejected the idea that they crushed shells.

facts.statement: In 2004, Lü and colleagues hypothesized that the skull bones of Nemegtomaia were movable relative to each other.
